source.title: Model, sample, and epoch-wise descents: exact solution of gradient flow in the random feature model

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: It analytically studies model-, sample-, and epoch-wise test-error behavior in a random feature model, using gradient flow rather than the cited deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's own analytical curves and simulation comparisons are included. Results cited from other work are not recorded. Parameter values used to illustrate a curve are recorded as conditions only when the text links them to a reported outcome.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact time-evolution curves of test error for gradient flow in a high-dimensional random feature model, checked against finite-d simulations. Its own results bear on model-wise (as a non-deep model class), sample-wise, epoch-wise and triple descent, and on regularization dependence. It is a different method aimed at the same question, and is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors derive exact analytical time evolution of training and test errors under gradient flow for the high-dimensional random feature model. They show that model- and sample-wise double and triple descents develop only after a definite time and are preceded by a dip, so early stopping helps in some regimes. They find two epoch-wise structures: a monotone double plateau when ψ≫φ, and a double-descent-like elongated bump. The analysis relies on an unproven concentration assumption but matches simulations.
record.recipe_differences: Analytical high-dimensional random feature model with fixed random first-layer weights and gradient flow, rather than empirical deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports distinct epoch-wise behavior by regime and parameter choice; large regularization removes double descent, and the epoch-wise bump is reported for selected noise and ratio settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Large λ adds a two-stage decrease in the training error (Figs. 9, 15, 16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ridge regularization induces multi-stage descents in training error under gradient flow.

record.problems: The authors state that the analysis is not fully mathematically controlled, chiefly because concentration is assumed. The central curves are analytical; empirical checks use finite-dimensional simulations, including 10-instance comparisons, and several reported curve values are only available in figures.

untested.parts: All of it; only a shallow random feature model with a fixed first layer is studied.
Deep networks and SGD/Adam training; only gradient flow in the random feature model is analysed.
Model classes other than random feature regression.
All of it; no effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak is not isolated. Optimally tuned regularization is not tested.

missing.what: The linear spike of the triple descent appears earlier in training than the nonlinear spike.
Noise dependence: the epoch-wise bump needs larger s and r; with r=0 the second plateau of test error vanishes.
Epoch-wise structures are more marked for a steeper activation, tanh(5x) versus tanh(x).
At fixed δ=cλ, the interpolation-threshold time scale becomes constant in the over-parameterized regime, which the authors call consistent with [22].

record.verdict_notes: Treated as T2: analytical theory plus finite-d simulation checks. V1 is not tested because the model is shallow; the model-wise result is credited to V4 as one non-deep model class. R7 was changed from absent to observed, because removal of the peak by regularization is what V6 predicts. The V6 R7 label was changed from limits_scope to supports; optimal tuning is listed as untested.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses a shallow random feature model, not deep networks, so it does not test the deep-network-specific claim.
Deep-network training and empirical optimizer settings are not tested; the study analyzes gradient flow in a random feature model.
The sample-size sweep is in the random feature model, not deep networks.
The study tests a random feature model only, not a broad sweep across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested as predicting peak location across axes.
The study reports multiple descents and regularization dependence, but does not establish that label noise or variance drives the peak, or test optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters.
